name: Avocado
summary: This guide shows how Filipino growers usually raise avocado from the seed of a good fruit, plant it out and care for it until the first fruits, with notes on grafted seedlings. It is for backyards and small orchards.
season: Planting can be done in any month, but the best time is the start of the rainy season, around May to July. Trees planted in the dry season need watering and some shade. The fruiting season here runs about April to September.
material: In the old way, growers sow a big, fresh seed from a tasty fruit of a healthy, heavy bearing tree, pointed end up with about a quarter of the seed above the soil. It sprouts in about 2 to 3 weeks. Trees from seed do not come true and take about 4 to 5 years to bear. Grafted seedlings of a named variety on a seedling rootstock come true and bear much earlier, and most orchard growers now use them.
spacing: About 9 m between trees each way, roughly 120 to 125 trees a hectare. Backyard trees are planted wherever there is enough room for a big crown.
water: Mostly rain fed, but young trees need regular water in the dry months of their first 2 or 3 years, about every two weeks. Water matters most where the dry season lasts more than 4 to 5 months. Avocado cannot stand waterlogged soil.
fertilizer: Compost or manure in the hole. About 100 to 200 g of ammonium sulfate (21 0 0) or 50 to 100 g of urea (46 0 0) a tree one month after planting, repeated every six months and increased as the tree grows. When fruiting starts, about 500 g of complete fertilizer (14 14 14) a tree twice a year. Big bearing trees get at least 2 kg a year, split between the start and the end of the rains.
care: Shading and watering young trees, weeding around them, growing short crops or a legume cover between the trees, light pruning of dead or sick branches only, and checking the trunk for borers and the leaves for caterpillars and bugs. Keeping drainage good to avoid root rot.
harvest: The season here runs about April to September. Fruit is mature when green kinds turn light green, purple kinds show reddish streaks, and the fruit sounds hollow when tapped. Pick with a pole fitted with a hook and net, never letting fruit drop, and ripen it in the shade for a few days. A grown tree can give several hundred fruits a year.

ways.label: Seedling from seed, or grafted seedling (punla o grafted)

steps.title: Sow the seed in a bag
steps.how: Wash a big, fresh seed and sow it in a bag of loose soil with the pointed end up and about a quarter of it showing. Keep the bag in light shade and water it so the soil stays moist. It sprouts in about 2 to 3 weeks.

steps.title: Clear the land and mark the spots
steps.how: Clear and loosen the ground, and mark the planting spots about 9 m apart each way. Choose a spot that drains well, since avocado roots rot in wet soil.

steps.title: Dig the holes
steps.how: Dig each hole wide and deep enough to hold the whole soil ball of the seedling with room to spare. Mix the topsoil with compost or dried manure for filling back.

steps.title: Plant the seedling
steps.how: Plant when the seedling is about 50 cm tall. Remove the bag gently, set the plant at the same depth it grew, keep any graft union above the soil and press the soil firmly around the base.

steps.title: Shade and water
steps.how: Give the young tree some shade if the sun is hot, and water it regularly in dry months. In the first 2 or 3 years, water about every two weeks during the dry season.

steps.title: First fertilizer
steps.how: One month after planting, spread about 100 to 200 g of ammonium sulfate (21 0 0), or about 50 to 100 g of urea (46 0 0), around the tree and mix it into the soil. Repeat every six months, a little more each time. Use less if you add manure or compost.

steps.title: Weed and plant crops between
steps.how: Keep the circle around the young tree free of weeds. Banana, papaya, pineapple, corn or vegetables can grow in the space between trees while they are small.

steps.title: Check for borers and leaf eaters
steps.how: Look at the trunk for borer holes and at the leaves for caterpillars and sucking bugs. Dig out borer larvae from the wounds and remove dead or rotting branches.

steps.title: Second fertilizer
steps.how: Six months after the first feeding, give the same or a little more ammonium sulfate or urea. Keep feeding twice a year as the tree grows.

steps.title: Light pruning only
steps.how: Remove only dead, broken or sick branches. On varieties that shoot straight up, cut the top lightly so the tree spreads sideways.

steps.title: First fruits
steps.how: Pick when green types turn lighter green or purple types show reddish streaks, and the fruit sounds hollow when tapped. Use a picking pole with a hook and net so the fruit does not fall, then let it soften in the shade.

ways.note: A tree from seed bears at about 4 to 5 years. A grafted tree bears earlier. The nursery step is counted back from the planting day.

mistakes: Planting in low, wet ground where the roots rot.
Expecting a tree from seed to give the same fruit as its mother.
Letting young trees dry out in their first dry seasons.
Pruning hard every year, which cuts off the fruiting wood.
Shaking fruit down or letting it drop, so it bruises and rots.
Ignoring trunk borers until the bark dies.
better: Plant grafted seedlings of a proven variety from an accredited nursery for earlier, even fruit.
Test the soil and feed by the result, with complete fertilizer once the tree bears.
Plant on well drained ground or mounds and keep canals clear in the rainy season.
Water young trees every two weeks in the dry months for the first 2 or 3 years.
Scout for borers, fruit flies and leaf spots and clean up fallen fruit.
Plant two or more varieties near each other for better fruit set.

watering.traditional: Avocado here is mostly rain fed: young trees get a pail or a hose about every two weeks in the dry months of their first two or three years, and grown trees are left to the rain. Water matters most where the dry season runs longer than four to five months, because avocado flowers in the dry months.
watering.method: A pail or hose into a wide ring basin for young trees. Grown trees get rain, and a few commercial orchards use drip or small sprinklers. Avocado is easily hurt by salty water, so use clean water. Water early in the morning.
watering.rainfed: Plant as the rains begin, shade the young tree from hot sun, and keep a thick mulch of rice straw, dry leaves or wood chips over the root area, off the trunk. A grown avocado needs at least about 100 to 130 cm of rain a year, well spread. Where the dry season is short, mulch carries it, and where it is long, the trees flower and set poorly without water.
watering.dryseason: Young trees: every one to two weeks. Bearing trees: every 7 to 10 days from flowering through fruit growth when no rain falls. Keep the top 15 to 20 cm of soil moist. Water when the leaves droop in the afternoon or their tips start to brown.
watering.wet: Avocado roots rot fast in wet soil, and root rot is the main killer of avocado trees. Plant on a mound or a slope that drains, dig drains out of low spots, never flood the basin, and keep mulch off the trunk. Both too much and too little water bring on root rot, so water by the soil, not by the calendar.

schedule.often: Every day or every other day, in light shade
schedule.amount: Enough to keep the bag soil moist, never soggy
schedule.why: The seed sprouts in two to three weeks only in steady moisture.

schedule.often: Water on planting day, then about twice a week when no rain falls. Shade the tree from hot sun
schedule.amount: One to two watering cans a tree, into a ring basin away from the stem
schedule.why: The small root ball dries fast, and avocado roots are weak at finding water.

schedule.often: Every one to two weeks in the dry months, more often on sandy soil or in a hot spell
schedule.amount: Two to five watering cans (about 20 to 75 liters) a tree each time as it grows
schedule.why: Young trees planted in dry places die or stall without this.

schedule.often: Every 7 to 10 days in long dry spells
schedule.amount: A deep soak that wets the top 20 to 60 cm of soil under the crown, where most roots are
schedule.why: A full, healthy crown carries the first crop.

schedule.stage: Flowering and fruit set (each year, mostly in the dry months)
schedule.often: Every 7 to 10 days if no rain falls
schedule.amount: A deep soak under the whole crown
schedule.why: This is the most critical stage: dry soil drops flowers and small fruits.

schedule.often: Every 7 to 10 days in dry spells, until the rains take over
schedule.amount: A deep soak under the crown
schedule.why: Steady moisture gives bigger fruits. The season here runs about April to September.

critical: The first year after planting, when young trees die quickly in the dry months.
Flowering and fruit set, the stage when lack of water causes the heaviest fruit drop.
Fruit growth in the dry months, which decides fruit size.

signs.dry: Leaves droop in the afternoon, their tips and edges turn brown and burnt, older leaves fall, and flowers and small fruits drop.
signs.wet: Small, pale yellow leaves, wilting even though the soil is wet, branches dying back from the top, and brown, brittle roots with few fine feeder roots.

better: A thick, coarse mulch over the whole root area and drip or small sprinklers that wet that area from flowering to fruit growth give a much better fruit set.
Plant on mounds and water only when the top soil dries. It keeps root rot away better than any spray.
